insight.title: Bananas Are Shipped Completely Asleep
insight.subtitle: Supermarkets don't buy ripe fruit—they trigger ripening inside sealed gas chambers right before delivery.
insight.notificationHook: Bananas travel in a chemical coma

sections.text: Bananas are the world's most sold grocery item, yet they never ripen on the tree. They are picked green, packed into airtight containers, and placed into a cold, low-oxygen state.
This artificial hibernation pauses aging during weeks of ocean travel. Once docked, trucks deliver dormant fruit to local ripening rooms, where precise blasts of ethylene gas wake them up on command.
Controlling the exact hour fruit wakes up eliminates waste, synchronizes harvests across continents, and guarantees millions of bananas hit store shelves at the exact same shade of yellow.
Global logistics doesn't just move produce. It pauses time.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Five tech giants have committed more than three trillion dollars to future spending on artificial intelligence. Bloomberg reported that Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle signed deals for energy, leases, and equipment. Alphabet led spending commitments with more than one trillion dollars, nearly eight times its level last year. Meta pledged over 800 billion dollars, with nearly half for data centre leases not yet started. Future leases make up 1.3 trillion dollars of the total, while other orders equal 1.9 trillion dollars. Meta and Alphabet both moved into negative free cash flow because of this spending. Analytics firm Gartner warned that much of this spending may never pay off.

Turning to international trade, India cut its oil imports from the United States to zero in September 2026. Official data shows India also reduced crude oil imports from Russia by nearly 18 percent. President Donald Trump signed the Russia Sanctions Act into law on September 18. That law allows tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries buying Russian oil. To replace that oil, India increased imports from the United Arab Emirates by 67 percent. The United Arab Emirates supplied 26.5 percent of India's oil in September, an all-time high. Official Indian government data on October oil imports will be released next month.

In economic news, Taiwan reported its fourth straight quarter of double-digit economic growth on October 30. The statistics bureau in Taipei said gross domestic product grew 14.36 percent in the third quarter. That is Taiwan's longest stretch of high growth in nearly 39 years. Exports jumped almost 61 percent in September to a record of over 87 billion dollars. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reported a 69 percent profit jump for July through September. Taiwan's Cabinet proposed a record spending plan of 3.93 trillion New Taiwan dollars for 2027. Under that proposal, overall military spending would exceed three percent of economic output.

Next, nearly 200 nations approved two major environmental agreements at a United Nations summit in Armenia. The two-week summit in Yerevan aimed to revive goals to stop nature destruction by 2030. Delegates agreed to accelerate efforts after the United Nations warned that progress was insufficient. The United Nations target calls for protecting 30 percent of Earth's land and oceans by 2030. Disagreements remained over conservation funding and tackling subsidies that harm the environment. The European Union asked wealthy emerging economies like China to contribute money to conservation efforts. Key decisions on the Cali Fund for conservation were delayed for two years.

In legal news, Meta reached a settlement with an 18-year-old plaintiff over social media addiction claims. The teenager claimed that platforms like Instagram contributed to severe depression and anxiety. Jury selection was scheduled to start on October 29 in Los Angeles Superior Court. Meta agreed to settle to avoid going to trial, according to the plaintiff's lawyer. Legal proceedings will still move forward against Snapchat owner Snap Incorporated. Thousands of other lawsuits accuse tech firms of creating features that promote compulsive usage. In March, a Los Angeles jury awarded six million dollars in a similar case. Meta also faces a 25 billion dollar penalty in New Mexico, which it plans to appeal.

Turning to diplomacy, Group of 20 foreign ministers opened talks in the United States on Friday amid deep rifts. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov of presenting lies. Kallas said European leaders pushed back against Lavrov's false narratives about Ukraine. European diplomats also rejected a group photo op with the Russian official. United States official Marco Rubio held separate sideline talks with Lavrov in Atlanta. Russia showed no sign on Friday of softening its stance regarding Ukraine. Sharp disagreements emerged around the table between European diplomats and Russian representatives.

Next, we turn to a Treasury report on how U.S. blockade sanctions are crippling Iran's economy.

A Treasury Department report says U.S. actions have crippled Iran's economy, according to Axios. The report points to a U.S. naval blockade and sweeping economic sanctions. It also notes that overland export routes have been blocked. These actions have increased economic pressure on Iran's government. The document was obtained by the news website Axios.

Turning to technology, tech stocks dropped sharply on Friday as major companies increased AI spending. Shares of Intel, the chip maker, fell by twenty-eight percent. Alphabet, the owner of Google, dropped another one point four percent. The Nasdaq index ended October with its worst monthly drop since March 2025. Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committed eight hundred billion dollars total for 2026. Alphabet expects to spend up to two hundred five billion dollars this year on investments. Amazon committed to spending two hundred twenty billion dollars this year on equipment and data centers. The Nasdaq is still up seven point eight percent over the last year.

In international news, Italian inflation rose to five point four percent in October during national strikes. Statistics agency Istat reported that energy prices increased thirty-one point four percent from last year. Italian inflation is now higher than the United States rate of three point seven percent. Farmers and truckers blocked roads to protest high diesel costs. The blockades stopped food deliveries, leaving supermarket shelves empty across southern Italy. About one million liters of milk went unused in a single day, a consortium director said. Pasta maker Rummo suspended production, while La Molisana halted its plant. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government approved a one hundred seventy-five point two million euro aid package.

On space news, the United States, Russia, and China are working to put nuclear reactors on the moon. NASA plans to develop its first lunar reactor by the end of 2030. NASA's reactor is designed to produce twenty kilowatts of electricity for five years. Russia and China aim to place a ten kilowatt reactor there by 2036. The reactors will power lunar bases and heavy water mining operations. Scientists plan to extract frozen water to create drinking water, air, and rocket fuel. Solar power is limited because areas on the moon go dark for two weeks. Both the United States and Russia say reactors will remain off until landing.

In business news, a data breach affected reservation records for Cathay Pacific passengers, the airline said. An unauthorized party accessed information stored by third-party technology provider Amadeus IT Group. The accessed data included passenger names, booking references, and flight details. Cathay Pacific said there is no evidence that payment details were accessed. The breach occurred between August 2023 and September 2026 using system credentials. Japan Airlines reported that ninety-two thousand of its customers were also affected. ANA Holdings reported about thirty-seven thousand eight hundred affected passengers. Cathay Pacific confirmed it has informed relevant authorities about the incident. Amadeus reset passwords and stated that it found no evidence of data misuse.

Finally, Tesla and one hundred thirteen other profitable companies paid no current federal income tax last year. A report from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy analyzed company financial filings. The report showed over seven hundred corporations paid an effective tax rate of ten point four percent. That is less than half of the official twenty-one percent federal corporate tax rate. Corporate tax revenue dropped fifteen percent to three hundred eighty-one billion dollars last fiscal year. Think tank researcher Matt Gardner said reduced tax rates pose a larger threat than zero-tax companies. Seven hundred six companies saved one hundred ninety-eight billion dollars last year through tax subsidies.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Bananas are the world's most sold grocery item, but they never ripen on the tree. Workers pick them green and pack them into cold, low-oxygen containers. This state pauses their aging during weeks of ocean travel. After arriving, trucks deliver the dormant fruit to local ripening rooms. Special blasts of ethylene gas wake the bananas up on command. This process controls the exact hour fruit ripens and eliminates waste. It allows millions of bananas to reach store shelves at the exact same shade of yellow. It is fascinating how global supply chains can pause time for our everyday food. When you hold a yellow banana, do you ever wonder how many weeks it spent asleep?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of today's biggest global stories.

Why are tech companies spending trillions of dollars on artificial intelligence? Five technology companies recently promised more than three trillion dollars for future computer infrastructure.

Artificial intelligence takes a large amount of computing power. To build these systems, companies need specialized facilities called data centers. They also need computer chips and large amounts of electricity. For years, technology companies spent heavily to build up this infrastructure. In July, four top firms had pledged about two point four trillion dollars. Those companies were Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon. Alphabet owns Google, while Meta owns Facebook and Instagram. They competed to build the best artificial intelligence tools. However, computer chips require advanced factories to make them. Intel is a chipmaker based in the United States. It missed out on the early artificial intelligence boom. In March 2025, Intel hired a new chief executive officer named Lip-Bu Tan. He started a campaign to revive the company. The United States government also took a ten percent stake in Intel over a year ago. Chip maker Nvidia also bought a large stake in Intel.

Now, future spending promises have pushed some tech firms into negative cash flow. At the same time, unexpected delays and weak sales hit chipmakers.

Bloomberg reports five tech giants committed over three trillion dollars in future spending. These firms are Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle. Alphabet leads with more than one trillion dollars committed. Meta follows with over eight hundred billion dollars. Meta chief financial officer Susan Li said the firm expects to keep investing aggressively. Future leases make up one point three trillion dollars of the total spending. Other orders account for one point nine trillion dollars. Research firm Gartner warned much of this spending may never pay off. Alphabet and Meta now have negative free cash flow. Oracle said it expects positive cash flow again in 2028. Meanwhile, Intel stock fell twenty-nine percent on Friday. That was its worst day since the 1970s. The fall erased about twelve billion dollars from the government's holding value. It also cut Nvidia's stake value by about six billion dollars. Intel suffered an explosion at a factory in Israel. Intel finance chief David Zinsner said the incident killed two workers. It also seriously injured a third worker. Tan called the explosion an unfortunate and tragic accident that caused an extended shutdown. Zinsner said the shutdown will cost six hundred million dollars in lost revenue over two quarters. Global personal computer shipments fell four percent in the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. Amazon stock fell one point four percent after missing earnings expectations. The Nasdaq stock index fell two point nine percent for the week.

Investors are growing nervous about whether these investments will pay off. Spending keeps rising while some tech sales are slowing down.

Market strategist Matt Orton at Raymond James said this is not a moment of reckoning. He noted investors should think carefully because trading in the space remains crowded. Intel is making chips at its new plant in Arizona. However, Intel still has no external customers for those chips. Investors will watch to see if Intel announces new customers in the next two quarters.

Moving to our next story, changes in trade rules are reshaping global oil markets.

Why did India stop buying oil from the United States in September? India imported zero American crude oil in September after the United States passed new sanctions against Russia.

India buys large amounts of foreign oil to power its economy. Crude oil is untreated petroleum that countries refine into gasoline and other fuels. For a long time, Middle Eastern nations supplied most of India's crude oil. Then, Russia invaded Ukraine, which caused Western nations to limit Russian oil sales. Russia began offering discounts on its crude oil to attract buyers. So, India started buying large amounts of discounted Russian oil. In February, the United States removed penal tariffs linked to Russian oil imports. After that, India bought even more oil from Russia. By July 2026, Russian oil made up fifty-one percent of India's total oil imports. That was an all-time high share for Russia. At the same time, fighting in West Asia closed the Strait of Hormuz. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway where much of the world's oil travels. That closure created supply constraints from traditional Middle Eastern shipping routes. Meanwhile, American oil averaged just over five percent of Indian imports over the previous year.

Then, American lawmakers decided to punish countries buying large amounts of Russian energy.

On September 16, the United States House of Representatives passed a new sanctions law. President Donald Trump signed the law on September 18. The law allowed tariffs of up to one hundred percent on countries buying Russian energy. Official data shows India slashed its American oil imports to zero in September 2026. India also cut its imports of Russian oil by nearly eighteen percent compared to August. Russia's share of Indian oil imports fell to thirty-three percent in September. Instead, India turned to the United Arab Emirates to replace the missing oil. Imports from the United Arab Emirates grew sixty-seven percent in September compared to August. That was a rise of one hundred nine percent compared to September of last year. The United Arab Emirates reached a record twenty-six point five percent share of India's oil imports. Together, Russia and the United Arab Emirates supplied sixty percent of India's oil in September. India imported two hundred nine point four lakh tonnes of crude oil that month. A lakh is an Indian numbering unit that means one hundred thousand. That total volume was nine point five percent higher than in August. However, India's monthly oil bill rose sixteen point four percent to nearly fourteen point three billion dollars. That bill was thirty-three percent higher than in September 2025 due to elevated oil prices.

India changed its oil suppliers right when the new American sanctions law took effect. Indian leaders wanted to avoid high tariffs while keeping their country supplied with energy.

The tariffs are currently in abeyance. President Trump signed an executive order on October 16 temporarily waiving the tariffs. He submitted a certification to Congress saying the pause was in the national interest. Next month, the Indian government will release official oil import figures for October. Those numbers will show if India starts buying American oil again or stays with the United Arab Emirates.

Let's turn now to another part of Asia, where technology demand is driving economic growth.

How is the global artificial intelligence boom transforming Taiwan's economy? Taiwan recorded its fourth straight quarter of double-digit economic growth due to high global demand for technology.

Taiwan is an island in East Asia known for high-tech manufacturing. It is home to advanced microchip factories. Microchips are tiny electronic circuits that power computers, smartphones, and artificial intelligence systems. For decades, global electronics companies have relied on Taiwanese factories to make their components. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is the world's largest contract maker of advanced chips. It produces critical hardware for technology companies like Nvidia and Apple. In recent years, artificial intelligence applications expanded rapidly around the world. Building these complex systems requires large amounts of advanced processing chips. As a result, tech companies ordered record numbers of hardware components from Taiwanese suppliers. This foreign demand created an economic expansion across the island. Over time, the money flowing into tech companies started spreading into the broader local economy. Local workers earned more, which increased domestic shopping and consumer spending.

That momentum pushed Taiwan into its longest run of high economic growth in nearly four decades.

Taiwan's statistics bureau reported that gross domestic product grew fourteen point three six percent in the third quarter. Gross domestic product measures the total value of all goods and services produced by a country. That growth rate beat the median estimate of twelve percent from a survey of economists by Bloomberg. It marks Taiwan's fourth consecutive quarter of double-digit economic growth. The statistics bureau noted this is the longest stretch of such growth since 1987. In September, Taiwan's exports surged almost sixty-one percent. Total exports reached a record of over eighty-seven billion U.S. dollars. That total beat forecasts from every economist surveyed by Bloomberg. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reported a sixty-nine percent profit jump from July through September. The chipmaker also delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook for the fourth quarter. This economic expansion boosted public finances for the Taiwanese government. The Cabinet proposed a record three point nine three trillion New Taiwan dollar spending plan for 2027. That budget gives the government more room to fund priorities including defense. Under the proposal, overall military spending would exceed three percent of Taiwan's gross domestic product.

Global tech firms are buying vast amounts of hardware to build artificial intelligence systems right now. That spending boom is driving sales for Taiwanese factories.

This growth gives Taiwan extra tax revenue to fund its military defense programs. However, concerns persist over whether the artificial intelligence investment boom can be sustained. If tech companies cut back on hardware orders, Taiwan's rapid economic growth could slow down. Observers will watch upcoming financial reports to see if foreign chip demand remains strong into next year.

Up next, nations commit to get nature goals back on track at a United Nations biodiversity summit.

Can world leaders agree to save nature before it is too late? At a summit in Armenia, nearly two hundred nations approved new agreements to protect plants and animals.

Earth is losing plants and animals because people clear forests, pollute rivers, and overfish oceans. So, nations created the United Nations biodiversity process to set global goals. Biodiversity means the wide variety of all living things on Earth. In 2022, countries set targets for 2030, like protecting thirty percent of Earth's land and oceans. They also promised to tackle pollution, control invasive species, and boost funding for conservation. Invasive species are foreign plants or animals that harm local wildlife. However, progress was insufficient to meet those targets. Governments kept spending public money on subsidies. Subsidies are payments that lower costs for businesses. These payments encouraged activities harmful to nature, like fossil fuel use and intensive farming. At the same time, conservation funds remained far too low. Because of these delays, nature lost vital habitats year after year.

Leaders gathered in Yerevan, Armenia for two weeks of tough talks. The summit faced tense political arguments and disagreements over science. Several delegations even challenged scientific reports about nature loss. Swiss negotiator Gabriela Blatter said science is not negotiable. That shocked veteran observers who expected countries to respect scientific evidence. Still, delegates worked through extended hours to reach an agreement.

COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan approved two major final texts after late negotiations. Draft texts urged nations to accelerate efforts to tackle the forces driving biodiversity loss. Guido Broekhoven from WWF International called this outcome a step forward, despite weaknesses on harmful subsidies. An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International said the summit built political momentum against harmful subsidies. However, French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said progress was not commensurate with the crisis. She warned that nature will not wait for slow negotiations. Countries also failed to resolve questions about the Cali Fund. Pakhi Das from Plant-for-the-Planet said delay leaves the fund almost empty for two years. Finally, delegates voted secretly for Ecuador to host the next summit in 2028 after defeating Panama.

This summit happened now because the 2030 deadline is approaching quickly. Also, global economic troubles, an energy crisis, and ongoing wars have strained public budgets. Wealthy nations like the European Union wanted emerging economies like China to contribute money. Because public money is tight, finding cash for nature became urgent.

This matters because healthy ecosystems provide the food, clean water, and air we need to survive. If countries fail to stop biodiversity loss, prices for food could rise. Next, watch whether governments actually reduce harmful subsidies in their national budgets. Countries might voluntarily join donation groups before the next summit in 2028. Corporate contributions to the Cali Fund could also remain low until rules are settled.

While world leaders debate global policy, social media giants face growing legal battles at home.

Why is Meta settling lawsuits with teenagers who claim social media harmed their mental health? Meta reached a private settlement with an eighteen-year-old plaintiff right before a major court trial began.

Tech companies built social media apps with features like infinite scrolling and video autoplay. Infinite scrolling means news feeds continuously load new content without stopping. Teenagers began spending hours scrolling on these platforms instead of sleeping. The Mississippi plaintiff, known as K.D.B., described losing focus in class and engaging in self-harm. Plaintiffs claimed they started YouTube at age three and other platforms at age nine. Parents and young users noticed serious problems, including depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. Because of these harms, thousands of families and school districts filed lawsuits against tech companies. They accused companies of designing apps to foster compulsive usage among children. Social media companies denied these claims, saying they added safety tools for young users. In March, a Los Angeles jury handed down a landmark ruling. They found Meta and YouTube negligent and awarded six million dollars to a young woman. That verdict proved that tech companies could lose in court. So, tech companies began negotiating settlements to avoid risky public trials.

An eighteen-year-old woman from Mississippi brought a major case against Meta and Snap. Jury selection began in Los Angeles for her trial. But just before testimony started, Meta agreed to settle the case out of court.

Lawyer Emily Jeffcott confirmed the settlement, expressing pleasure at reaching a just resolution. Terms of the agreement were not disclosed, and Meta did not comment right away. Snap is now the only remaining defendant in this specific trial. A Snap spokesperson said Snapchat was built differently because it opens to a camera, not a feed. They added that safety tools protect users and that claims misrepresent the app. Snap Chief Executive Officer Evan Spiegel is expected to testify during the trial. Snap also recently settled a lawsuit over its speed filter after high-speed car crashes. This comes after Meta settled state lawsuits for up to eighteen billion dollars. A New Mexico court also penalized Meta twenty-five billion dollars over privacy, which Meta plans to appeal.

Meta settled right now because jury selection had already started in Los Angeles. Facing a multi-week public trial created financial and reputational risks for the company. By settling immediately, Meta avoids having its internal practices debated in open court.

This case matters because social media design affects millions of daily users. If courts hold tech giants responsible, companies might change app features to protect kids. Next, watch whether Evan Spiegel actually takes the stand to testify for Snap. That would mark the first time a Snap founder testifies in an addiction trial. Other legal cases could also end in settlements as platforms try to limit legal damage.

Legal battles at home are not the only diplomatic friction facing American leaders right now.

Why did top diplomats cancel their traditional group photograph at the G20 meeting in Atlanta? The United States canceled the photo after European diplomats refused to stand next to Russia's top diplomat.

Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, which caused Western nations to place heavy sanctions on Moscow. Sanctions are official penalties that restrict trade and business with a country. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was personally put under sanctions, isolating him from Western leaders. Meanwhile, hostilities broke out in West Asia. American and Israeli strikes on Iran led Tehran to block the Strait of Hormuz. The Strait of Hormuz is a vital waterway where much of the world's oil travels. Because shipping stopped, global energy costs rocketed, creating economic strain worldwide. The United States then assumed presidency of the Group of 20 economies. The Group of 20 is an organization of major economies including Japan, Germany, India, China, and France. Washington planned a foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta to prepare for a summit in Miami. However, deep divisions over war, tariffs, and shipping lanes made reaching agreements very difficult.

When diplomats arrived in Atlanta, European representatives threatened to boycott the official group photograph. They objected to appearing in a picture with Sergey Lavrov while Russia attacked Ukraine. To prevent a public dispute, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio scrapped the photo.

Marco Rubio hosted the two-day gathering in Atlanta just days before United States midterm elections. Russian state media reported that Sergey Lavrov attended to argue against international sanctions. Meanwhile, China sent a deputy foreign minister instead of its top diplomat Wang Yi. Two United States officials said Rubio canceled the photo to keep discussions moving forward. A diplomatic source noted that the G20 will likely publish a chair summary instead of a joint statement. Discussions focused on keeping sea lanes open without threats or tolls. Alisha Chhangani from the Atlantic Council called this meeting the last test case before Miami. Additionally, Washington granted entry to Flavio Bolsonaro after his defeat in Brazil's election.

This meeting happened now to set the stage for President Donald Trump's December summit in Miami. That summit will take place at his Doral resort before handing leadership to Britain. Also, United States midterm elections are taking place on Tuesday, November third. Washington wants to rein in fuel prices and show economic strength before voters go to the polls.

This friction matters because global energy prices directly affect fuel costs for consumers. Ongoing blockades in key waterways could keep energy prices high. Next, watch whether West Asia conflict escalates after Tuesday's midterm elections. President Donald Trump has signaled he could attack Iran after the vote. Observers will also watch if leaders agree on free navigation before the December summit in Miami.

Up next, a Treasury report shows how United States sanctions and a blockade are crippling Iran's economy.

New reports detail the economic strain on Iran from sanctions. The U.S. naval blockade, sweeping economic sanctions and obstruction of overland export routes have crippled Iran's economy and intensified pressure on the regime, according to a new Treasury Department report obtained by Axios. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is leading this economic effort.

Why are tech stocks falling when AI spending is near one trillion dollars? US tech stocks have tumbled for two days in a row because investors worry that companies are spending massive amounts of money on artificial intelligence without making enough profit back. 

For years, big technology companies have raced to build the internet and the cloud. They spent billions of dollars on servers and data centres. Then, a new kind of computer brain called artificial intelligence arrived. Companies wanted to win the race to build the smartest AI. They began spending huge piles of money to buy special computer chips and build giant new data centres to power the new technology. 

Now, the spending has grown so large that it is reaching about one trillion dollars. Big tech companies like Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committed to spending eight hundred billion dollars between them in 2026. 

Then came the change that turned the situation into news. Companies reported their money results for the latest three months, and many of them spent much more money than they made. Alphabet, which owns Google, revealed that its new AI search summaries were hurting its main search advertising revenue. Alphabet expects to spend up to two hundred and five billion dollars this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI. 

Today, the stock market has reacted sharply to these money reports. Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row. Shares in Intel plummeted by twenty-eight percent on Friday after the chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers. Intel shed more than one hundred and thirty billion dollars in value. Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another one point four percent after a twelve percent plunge on Thursday. Amazon shares dropped around five percent, and Reddit stock plunged by twenty-nine percent. The Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US ended October with its worst monthly slide since March twenty-twenty-five. 

This is happening now because it is the end of the month when big companies report their financial results to the public all at once. 

This could mean that the massive boom in artificial intelligence spending has reached its peak, and investors might look for a new theme to drive markets. Stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago, and the Nasdaq is still up seven point eight percent over the last year. Watch to see if tech stocks keep falling in the coming days.

Why did a farmers' revolt empty Italian supermarket shelves? Inflation in Italy rose to five point four percent in October, which is higher than in the US and far above China. 

For decades, Italian families have watched the cost of living climb higher. Prices for everyday food rose much faster than overall consumer prices since the year two thousand. Farmers and truckers felt squeezed by the high cost of running a farm, especially diesel fuel. Diesel costs roughly a third more than it did before the Iran war, and a temporary diesel tax discount recently ended. 

Then, the situation changed when truckers and farmers launched a month-long fight over these costs. They began blocking roads, ports, and fuel depots across the south of Italy in mid-October. 

Today, those blockades have cut off the supply of fresh food. Since buffalo mozzarella cheese must be made within sixty hours of milking, and trucks were stopped, milk could not reach dairies. About one million litres went unused in a single day, causing three million euros in losses in twenty-four hours. Pasta makers like Rummo and La Molisana suspended production because they ran out of ingredients. Supermarkets in Naples posted apologies on empty shelves, and Sicily ran short of fresh pasta, cheese, and meat because food rotted in warehouses. Protesters also marched through more than fifty Italian cities during a general strike, while Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government approved a one hundred and seventy-five point two million euro aid package for truckers, farmers, and fishermen to end the pickets. 

This is happening now because high energy prices and the end of tax discounts pushed costs too high for workers to bear. 

This means that high living costs are hurting everyday people and disrupting food supplies across southern Italy. Watch to see if food prices stay high or if more protests return.

Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?

Why are the United States, Russia, and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon? They want to power future moon bases and mine for water ice, but scientists warn of radioactive risks. 

Space exploration has a long history. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union launched more than thirty nuclear reactors into Earth's orbit to power spy satellites. The United States also spent twenty billion dollars on space nuclear programs over seventy years, but never successfully launched a reactor since an early test in 1965. 

Now, the countries want to build bases near the moon's south pole. This area has frozen water trapped deep in craters where sunlight never reaches. The water could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel. 

Solar power on the moon is limited because the sun only shines on any spot half the time. Solar panels would go dark for about two weeks every month. Batteries and diesel are too costly to launch from Earth, so nuclear energy is seen as the best choice. 

In January, NASA announced plans to develop a lunar reactor by the end of 2030. The United States transportation secretary said the country is in a race to the moon with China. Russia is also building a reactor called Selena, which will power a Chinese-led moon base by about 2036. 

NASA's reactor will produce twenty kilowatts of electricity and run for five years without maintenance. It will weigh under six thousand kilograms to fit inside a rocket. Russia's Selena reactor will produce ten kilowatts, run for a decade, and weigh between eleven hundred and thirteen hundred kilograms for a softer landing. 

Building the reactor is only the first step. The biggest challenge will be launching, landing, and setting up the system safely on the moon. 

If a reactor falls back to Earth, the risk is real. In 1978, a Soviet satellite carrying a reactor scattered radioactive material across northern Canada. On the moon, scientists say any contaminated area would be extremely localized. Legally, no one can claim the moon under a 1967 treaty, but countries own the equipment they send there. 

This could mean a permanent human presence on the moon, though launch delays or accidents remain possible. 

Next, travel reservation records held by a third-party service provider were accessed by an unauthorized person, affecting major airlines. Booking references, names, and flight details were exposed in most cases. 

Amadeus IT Group provides technology solutions to the travel industry. Between August 2023 and September 2026, an unauthorized party used log-in credentials to access the Amadeus system. Cathay Pacific learned of the breach from Amadeus and found that about 53,000 bookings were affected. A smaller subset of cases involved emails, phone contacts, travel documents, and frequent flyer numbers. Amadeus confirmed that financial information was not accessed. 

Amadeus took action by resetting passwords and adding monitoring capabilities. Cathay Pacific stated that its own systems and operations were not affected, and it is investigating the incident. 

Other airlines were also hit. Korean Air and Asiana Airlines issued alerts after being notified by Amadeus. Japan Airlines and Japan Transocean Air disclosed that about 92,000 customers were affected. ANA Holdings reported that about 37,800 passenger records were leaked. Jin Air said 1,454 passengers were compromised, and Bloomberg reported that German carrier Condor was affected. 

The breach happened because of third-party system access, which affected multiple global airlines at once. 

This means passengers on several airlines could face a risk of targeted scams using leaked contact details, and travelers should watch for updates from their airlines. 

Next, why did 114 companies pay no current federal income tax last year while corporate profits soared? Lower tax rates and new tax breaks allowed profitable corporations to reduce what they pay. 

Over the past few decades, the United States has cut corporate tax rates. In 2018, the rate dropped from 35 percent to 21 percent. Last July, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act extended this rate and made several tax breaks permanent. 

These breaks include immediate expensing for research and development costs and bonus depreciation for business property. Companies saved a total of 198 billion dollars last year from tax subsidies. 

Last year, more than 700 profitable corporations paid an effective federal income tax rate of 10.4 percent. That is less than half of the 21 percent statutory rate. More than 250 companies paid below seven percent. 

A total of 114 companies, including Tesla, Walt Disney, United Airlines, and DoorDash, paid no current federal income tax. Treasury Department data showed a 15 percent reduction in corporate tax revenue, dropping by about 70 billion dollars to 381 billion dollars in the fiscal year ending September 30. 

This drop is part of a more than 25 percent reduction in corporate revenue since 2024. Meanwhile, corporate profits reached a record 4.7 percentage trillion dollars for the past twelve months through mid-2026. 

Policy experts are concerned about the federal deficit. The Congressional Budget Office projected the new tax law would add 3.4 trillion dollars to the federal deficit over the next decade. 

Experts point out that hundreds of corporations paying a reduced rate present a bigger threat to revenue than the companies paying zero. Meta faced scrutiny for classifying AI data centers as experimental research to claim tax breaks. 

Supporters of the tax breaks argue they boost investments and economic growth. Critics argue higher taxes could reduce the deficit and fund public needs. 

This could mean ongoing debate over tax policy, and we may see future changes depending on who holds office. 

Before we go, here is your thought for the day. 

Bananas are the world's most sold grocery item, yet they never ripen on the tree. They are picked green, packed into airtight containers, and placed into a cold, low-oxygen state. 

This artificial hibernation pauses aging during weeks of ocean travel. Once docked, trucks deliver dormant fruit to local ripening rooms, where precise blasts of ethylene gas wake them up on command. 

Controlling the exact hour fruit wakes up eliminates waste, synchronizes harvests across continents, and guarantees millions of bananas hit store shelves at the exact same shade of yellow. 

Global logistics doesn't just move produce. It pauses time. 

It is a quiet wonder that your morning fruit is sleeping right up until the moment you want to eat it. What other everyday things are traveling through time right now? 

Thank you for listening to Sift In-Depth. Take care, and we will talk again soon.
